title: Advice Given to Anathapindika
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk's main teaching centers on understanding the interconnectedness of all phenomena, encouraging listeners to see that everything arises and ceases due to causes and conditions. This understanding is rooted in the concept of "emptiness," which refers to the lack of inherent existence or self-nature in all things. By recognizing this emptiness, practitioners can cultivate a deeper sense of freedom and joy, and ultimately find liberation from suffering.

sentences.text: Hi everybody.
This is actually a retake because I forgot to record at the original talk the other night.
So, just wanted to let you know.

In keeping with our fall offerings on the early discourses of the Buddha, I wanted to offer a sutra found in the Ekotara Agama and also the Majjhima Nikaya, which is the Middle Length Discourses, and the Madhyama Agama, all collections of early Buddhist texts.
In the Middle Length Discourses, this sutra is named Anattapinda Kovada Sutra, and it means advice for Anattapindika.
It's also called, in the Plum Village tradition, Muthiknathana, he named this sutra, Discourse on Teachings Being Given to the Sick.
I'm going to present this talk in a little bit of a different format today.
I wanted to give a short history of Anattapindika and talk about my first encounter with the sutra.

Then I'm going to be reading through the Plum Village version of the sutra, replacing loosely the wording from the other translations and using the one by Thay, Thich Nhat Hanh, in the way that it was presented to me, which was more of a meditation format, nice and relaxed, and really just let this sutra be absorbed by you.

I'll end with a paragraph on the sutra as it was translated in the Middle Length Discourses, translated by Bhikkhu Nanamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, very popular translator, just to offer a reference and comparison to Thay's translation.
I want to give you a little bit of history.
Anattapindika actually was a very favorite of mine.
I had a lot of affinity towards Anattapindika for his generosity.
Anattapindika was born Sudatta, and he was a wealthy merchant banker and philanthropist, perhaps the most wealthy in Savattha at the time, and one of the Buddha's greatest lay supporters.
And I read someplace that I think he ended up spending about two-thirds of his time, an interesting and much fuller story around how he met the Buddha and his lifelong devotion there.
There's really abundant information about his life, one of, I would say, one of the earliest followers and one of the people in that time of the Buddha that has the most recorded history.
So you can look at some more about his life and a lot of information.
A good place to start is Wikipedia, which has really pretty detailed history of his whole life and his meeting with the Buddha, which is really an interesting story too.

He was a relative of Sabuddhi, which is one of Buddha's principal disciples, and Anattapindika means one who gives alms to the unprotected, supposedly because of his reputation of loving to give for those in need.

The short version of this story is that he was out looking around, this is after he became a student of the Buddha's, he was out looking around for some land to offer for a monastery and a place for the Buddha to give discourses.
He found this beautiful park on the edge of town, and he talked to the prince who owned it, and the prince didn't want to sell it.
So Anattapindika convinced him by covering the grounds of the park with coins.
The prince did indeed give it to Anattapindika, and there was, I think there was one patch of land that was not included in the purchase, and the prince ended up giving that to Anattapindika.
So anyway, this is the Jetavana monastery that was built there, and the Jetta Grove, which is a very, very famous area.
I know you probably have heard of the Jetta Grove, and in fact most of the Buddha's discourses were given there.
There are a lot of resources about the Jetta Grove and in many different teachings.
If you want, you can read the Old Path, White Clouds, Story of Buddha's Life by Thich Nhat Hanh, too.
When I first heard this sutra, it was one of my earliest retreats.
I think it was actually my first retreat with Thich Nhat Hanh, with many people in Mandolin, Illinois.

His sister Chang Kong, Sister True Emptiness, who was his really right-hand person through all of those years, read this sutra to us in a very meditative way, really reading from the words of the discourse.
So I'm going to read it like that.
If you don't know who Sister Chang Kong was, again, she's like the right-hand person for Thay, and she worked alongside him tirelessly through the whole Vietnam War.
They set up many, many services.
I was going to say one more thing.
She was really the first member of Thay's core community, the Order of Inner Being, and she really is still a backbone.
Beautiful voice.
I still remember how sweet and tender that was as she offered the sutra.
I was really deeply touched by those words.
I feel like it really penetrated to my core and gave a lot of freedom.
This discourse has never left me.
The discourse includes a little bit of history, a little conversation about the visit with Anantapindika, and then it includes what they told Anantapindika.
So I want you to really relax, close your eyes during the meditation part.
It's a little bit repetitive, a little lengthy.
It covers all of the aspects of our being.
So hang in there and just relax.
This was given to Anantapindika as he was dying.
It takes us through all of the aspects of our conditioned world, and really touches on the unconditioned, the ultimate dimension as Thay puts it.
*The discourse on teachings being given to the sick.
I heard these words of the Buddha one time when the Lord was staying in the monastery in Jeddah Grove in Anantapindika's park near Sravasti.
At the time, the householder Anantapindika was seriously ill.
When the Venerable Sheriputra was told this, he immediately went to Ananda and said, "Brother Ananda, we must go visit the layman Anantapindika."*
*The Venerable Ananda put on his robe and, holding his bowl, went into the town of Sravasti with the Venerable Sheriputra to make the alms round.
The two of them stopped at every house until they came to the house of layman Anantapindika, and they went in to visit him.
After they sat down, the Venerable Sheriputra asked the layman Anantapindika, "How is your illness?
Is it getting better or worse?
Is the physical pain easing, or is it getting greater?"
The householder Anantapindika replied, "Venerable monks, it is not getting any better.
It just doesn't seem to be.
The pain is not easing.
It's getting greater all the time."
Sheriputra said, "Friend Anantapindika, let us now practice together the recollection of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.
The recollection goes like this.*
*The Buddha has gone to suchness.

It is fully and truly awakened, has perfected understanding and action, has arrived at true happiness, understands the nature of the world, is unequaled in understanding, has conquered the afflictions of human beings, is a teacher of gods and humans, and is the awakened one, the one who liberates the world.
The Dharma is the teaching of love and understanding that the Tathagata has expounded.
It is deep and lovely, worthy of the highest respect and very precious.
It is a teaching that cannot be compared to ordinary teachings.
It is a path of practice for the noble ones.
The Sangha is the community of practice guided by the teachings of the Tathagata.
The community is in harmony and within aspects of the practice it can be realized.*
*The community is respected and precious.
It practices the precepts and realizes concentration, insight and liberation.
The Sangha is the highest field of merit in the world.
Friend Anathapindika, if you recollect the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha in this way, the beneficial effects are beyond measure.
Recollecting in this way, you can put an end to the obstacles of wrong deeds and afflictions.
You can harvest a fruit that is fresh and sweet as the nectar of deathlessness.
Anyone practicing in the upright way like this of life who knows how to recollect the three jewels will have no chance of falling into the three lower realms but will be reborn as a human or god.*
So now please just relax and let this soak in.
*Friend Anathapindika, now is the time to practice the meditation on the six senses.*
*These eyes are not me.
I am not caught in these eyes.
These ears are not me.
I am not caught in these ears.
This nose is not me.
I am not caught in this nose.
This tongue is not me.
I am not caught in this tongue.
This body is not me.
I am not caught in this body.
This mind is not me.
I am not caught in this mind.
Now continue your meditation on the six sense objects.
These forms are not me.
I am not caught in these forms.*
*These sounds are not me.
I am not caught in these sounds.
These smells are not me.
I am not caught in these smells.
These tastes are not me.
I am not caught in these tastes.
These contacts with the body are not me.
I am not caught in these contacts with the body.
These thoughts are not me.
I am not caught in these thoughts.
Now continue your meditation on the six sense consciousnesses.
Sight is not me.
I am not caught in sight.
Hearing is not me.
I am not caught in hearing.
Consciousness based on the nose is not me.
I am not caught in consciousness based on the nose.
Consciousness based on the tongue is not me.
I am not caught in consciousness based on the tongue.
Consciousness based on the body is not me.
I am not caught in consciousness based on the body.
Consciousness based on the mind is not me.
I am not caught in consciousness based on the mind.
Now, continue your meditation on the six elements.*
*The earth element is not me.
I am not caught in the earth element.
The water element is not me.
I am not caught in the water element.
The fire element is not me.
I am not caught in the fire element.
The air element is not me.
I am not caught in the air element.
The space element is not me.
I am not caught in the space element.
The consciousness element is not me.
I am not caught in the consciousness element.
Now continue your meditation on the five aggregates.
Form is not me.
I am not limited by the form aggregate.
Feelings are not me.
I am not limited by the feelings aggregate.
Perceptions are not me.
I am not limited by the perceptions aggregate.
Mental formations are not me.
I am not limited by the mental formations aggregate.
Consciousness is not me.
I am not limited by the consciousness aggregate.
Now continue your meditation on the three times.
The past is not me.
I am not limited by the past.
The present is not me.
I am not limited by the present.
The future is not me.
I am not limited by the future.*
*Friend Anathapindika, everything arises and ceases due to causes and conditions.
In reality, the nature of everything is not born and does not die, does not come and does not go.
When eyes arise, they arise, but they do not come from anywhere.
When eyes cease to be, they cease to be, but they do not go anywhere.
Eyes are neither non-existent before they arrive. [unclear: "Thing that is"] comes to be because of combination of causes and conditions.
When the causes and conditions are not sufficient, eyes are absent.
The same is true of ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.*
*Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and thought.
Sight, hearing, smelling, tasting, somatosensory, and mind consciousness.
The six elements, the five aggregates, and the three times.
In the five aggregates, there is nothing that we can call eye, a person, a lifespan.
Ignorance is the inability to see this truth.
Because there is ignorance, there are wrong perceptions of formations.
Because there are wrong perceptions of formations, there is wrong consciousness.
Because there is wrong consciousness, there is a distinction between the perceiver and the perceived.
Because there is a distinction between the perceiver and perceived, there is a distinction between the six organs and the six objects of sense.
Because there is a distinction between this contact.
Because there is contact, there is feeling.
Because there is feeling, there is craving.
There is grasping, there is being, and then birth, death, and the inexpressible mass of suffering and grief.
Friend Anattapindaka, you have meditated that everything that arises is due to causes and conditions and does not have a separate self.
That is called the meditation on emptiness.
It is the highest and most profound meditation.*
*When he practiced to this point, the layman Anattapindaka began to cry and tears flowed down his cheeks.
Venerable Ananda asked him, "Friend, why are you crying?
Has your meditation not been successful?
Do you have some regret?"
The layman Anattapindaka replied, "Venerable Ananda, I do not regret anything.
The meditation has been most successful.
I am crying because I am so deeply moved.

I have been fortunate to be able to serve the Buddha and his community for many years, yet I have never heard a teaching so wonderful and precious as the teaching transmitted by the Venerable Shariputra today."
Then the Venerable Ananda said to the layman Anattapindaka, "Do you not know, friend, that the Buddha often gives this teaching to bhikkhus and bhikkhunis?"

The layman Anattapindaka replied, "Venerable Ananda, please tell the Buddha that there are also lay people with the capacity of listening, understanding, and putting into this practice the deep and wonderful teachings."*
*After listening and practicing with the two Venerable monks, Anattapindaka felt free and at ease and gave rise to the highest mind.
The Venerable Shariputra and Ananda bade him farewell and went back to the monastery.
Anattapindaka passed away and was born in the thirty-third heaven.*
So that version is translated by Thich Nhat Hanh from the Ikotara Agama in consultation with the Majjhima Nikaya and the Madhyama Agama 26.
I hope you enjoyed that.
I'd like to read a paragraph now of the translation found in the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle Length Discourses, so you have a sense of how it's worded there also.
This is the discourse number 143, like I said, advice to Anattapindaka.
And here's an example of that meditative section that I just read through.
Instead of "these eyes are not me, I am not caught in these eyes," it is translated, "I will not cling to the eye and my consciousness will not be dependent on the eye."
And it goes through the six sense bases, the sense objects, et cetera, in that way with that wording.
For me, when I heard this phrase in the Thich Nhat Hanh version, it had this great sense of freedom.
I think that Thich Nhat Hanh often exercises his understanding in ways that he thinks provide the best chance of understanding for the listener.
But of course, everyone is different.
And that was the first time I ever heard this sutra.
I also know that clinging is described in many of the early texts as the primary reason a person is not peaceful, and therefore the release of clinging is the primary way to peace.
So I understand how this interpretation and version can be very encouraging around letting go from a different angle.

The Middle Length Discourse translation also includes a lengthier discussion that was interesting on the discourse with much more in-depth information about what happens to Anantapindika after his death.
So that's interesting too.
I think it's really good to contrast and compare different translations when you have the availability, as we are going through the sutras, the sutra study.
It's really good to see the differences.
Some are subtle, some are pretty substantial, and really get a feel for how you react and how they hit you.
I think it's really important to question the various interpretations and use logic as we're deciphering the translations.
It's also really good, I think, to know the background of the editor and translator.
For instance, I tend to be a little skeptical if the translation is purely from an academic view and not one that's accompanied by wisdom and direct experience from practice.
So it's really interesting.
And all these things hit us at different times, definitely, in our different lives.
There's one other thing.

Oh, and then the person that is actually doing the translating, if they come from a different cultural background than the early discourse, there's always differences in cultural understanding and we can't get away from that.
So that too is something to keep in mind.
Cultural and also time is very different, different times, different settings, different sutras have the flavor of those.
So anyway, I hope you enjoyed this discourse.

In the real-time version of this, we got into small groups and reflected on anything that struck us within the sutra, or maybe an awareness, as you heard this, of things coming up in body or mind from the words.
So I thank you for receiving the offering of the Sutra on Anattapindaka today.
I'm very grateful.
Thank you very much.
